prompt: Which property defines a service, in the sense this lesson uses?
hint: The one the other three serve.

choices.text: Being small enough for one person to read in an afternoon
choices.why: Size is the common misreading; a large program can be a service.

choices.text: Independent deployment
choices.why: Right. A new version goes out without any other service being rebuilt or told.

choices.text: Running in a container of its own
choices.why: Two containers that must always be deployed together are still one service.

choices.text: Speaking HTTP to the others
choices.why: The pipe can be HTTP or a queue; it is not what defines the service.

prompt: "Smart endpoints, dumb pipes" means what, for Quitanda's shop and stock services?
hint: Where should the decision "is there enough stock?" live?

choices.text: The network between them should route requests by sku and refuse orders for products that are out of stock
choices.why: That puts business logic in the pipe, which is what the phrase warns against.

choices.text: The stock service decides; HTTP only carries the request and the answer
choices.why: Right. The logic is in the services.

choices.text: Both services should be as simple as possible
choices.why: The endpoints are where the logic is meant to be.

choices.text: The shop should not validate anything it sends
choices.why: The phrase is about the pipe, not about skipping validation.

prompt: Match what a service buys to what it pays with.
hint: The second table of the first section.

pairs.right: a network call where a function call was

pairs.left: scaling one part on its own
a fault that stays in one service
pairs.right: the other service slow, gone or half done

pairs.left: each service in its own language
pairs.right: one more pipeline, image and alert

right_distractors: a shorter test suite for the whole system

prompt: Why does the lesson argue against one "product service" for Quitanda?
hint: Ask the catalogue, stock and delivery what a product is.

choices.text: A product table is too large for one database
choices.why: Size has nothing to do with it.

choices.text: Products change too often to be cached
choices.why: Caching is not the argument.

choices.text: The word means three things, and one service would hold all three
choices.why: Right. Every change to any meaning would be a change to it.

choices.text: Services should never be named after a noun
choices.why: Services are named after capabilities; the problem is holding several meanings, not the name.

prompt: Eric Evans called the area inside which a word has one precise meaning and one model a bounded ___.
hint: Domain-Driven Design, 2003.

prompt: The order and the stock must never disagree, not even for a second. What does the third question of the section say about a boundary between them?
hint: What needs one transaction?

choices.text: They belong in one service
choices.why: Right, or the disagreement has to be paid for in code, which is lesson 14.

choices.text: They should be split, with a faster network between the two halves
choices.why: A faster network still leaves two transactions that can disagree.

choices.text: They should share a database and keep two separate services on top of it
choices.why: That is the shared-database shortcut, with all its coupling.

choices.text: The question does not apply to stock
choices.why: It applies to any data that must agree at the same instant.

prompt: What does Conway's law predict about a company with three teams?
hint: 1968, communication structures.

choices.text: It will build a monolith, because three teams cannot agree
choices.why: The law is about the shape of the system following the teams.

choices.text: Its system will end up in three parts
choices.why: Right, wherever the natural boundaries of the problem lie.

choices.text: It needs at least three services per team to stay productive
choices.why: Nothing in the law counts services per team.

choices.text: Its teams will merge into one within a year
choices.why: The law describes systems, not how teams change.

prompt: Which of these are signs that a line between two services is in the wrong place? Choose all that apply.
hint: Four signs close the section.

choices.text: They call each other on nearly every request, both ways
choices.why: Right.

choices.text: A change needs a coordinated release of both
choices.why: Right.

choices.text: Each one has its own database
choices.why: That is how it should be.

choices.text: One keeps a copy of the other's data and the copies disagree
choices.why: Right.

choices.text: They are written in different languages
choices.why: Different languages are allowed, and often the point.

prompt: How does the shop container reach the stock service in the lab?
hint: Look at STOCK_URL in compose.yaml.

choices.text: Through port 8001 published on the machine's loopback
choices.why: The stock service publishes no port at all.

choices.text: By opening `stock.db` from the shared volume
choices.why: There is no shared volume; each service has its own.

choices.text: By the name `stock` on the Compose network
choices.why: Right: `http://stock:8001`, resolved by Docker inside the project's network.

choices.text: Through a message queue between them
choices.why: The lab's services talk HTTP; queues are lesson 6.

prompt: What is the `X-Request-Id` header for in the lab's two services?
hint: Look at the two log lines of `order-1`.

choices.text: It authenticates the shop to the stock service
choices.why: Nothing checks it; it identifies a request, not a caller.

choices.text: It prevents the same order from being placed twice
choices.why: It is not checked for duplicates; lesson 7 covers that problem.

choices.text: It joins the log lines of one order in both logs
choices.why: Right. With many services it is the only way to follow one request.

choices.text: It tells the stock service which product to take
choices.why: The product is in the path, `/stock/tomato/take`.

prompt: The order `order-1` bought 3 kg of tomatoes at 899 cents each. What `total_cents` did the shop answer?
hint: Price times quantity.

prompt: The catalogue needs the units of five products. Why does `do_GET` make one call to `/stock` instead of five calls to `/stock/<sku>`?
hint: What did each HTTP call cost in the bench?

choices.text: Five calls would be refused by the stock service
choices.why: The service answers single counts too; that is `/stock/<sku>`.

choices.text: Each call costs milliseconds, so one beats five
choices.why: Right. Lesson 16 calls the many-small-calls habit chatty I/O.

choices.text: One call is atomic and five calls are not, so the counts could change halfway through the list
choices.why: That can happen, but the lesson's reason is the cost per call.

choices.text: The shop is not allowed to know which skus exist
choices.why: It lists them from its own products table.

prompt: In the lab's bench, the HTTP call took 1809.60 µs and the function call 0.10 µs. How many times longer was the HTTP call? Round to the nearest thousand.
hint: Divide one by the other.

prompt: The shop sends a take request and no answer arrives before the timeout. What can the shop conclude?
hint: Which steps look identical from the caller's side?

choices.text: The units were not taken, since nothing came back
choices.why: The answer may have been lost after the units were taken.

choices.text: The units were taken, since the request was sent
choices.why: The request may never have arrived.

choices.text: Nothing certain, either way
choices.why: Right. The take may or may not have happened, and that uncertainty is what lesson 7 is about.

choices.text: The stock service has crashed and must be restarted
choices.why: A lost packet or a slow answer looks the same as a crash.

prompt: Which of these is one of the fallacies of distributed computing?
hint: Assumptions that were true inside the monolith.

choices.text: Services must have their own database
choices.why: That is a design rule, not a false assumption.

choices.text: Latency is zero
choices.why: Right, the second on Deutsch's list.

choices.text: HTTP is slower than function calls
choices.why: That is true, and the bench measured it.

choices.text: Containers share the host's kernel
choices.why: That is true of containers and has nothing to do with the list.

prompt: A page lists 40 products and asks the stock service once per product, each call taking 2 ms. How many milliseconds does the page spend on those calls, done one after the other?
hint: Forty times two.

prompt: With the stock container stopped, what did the catalogue request return in the lab?
hint: The transcript, and how long it took.

choices.text: A 503, in a few milliseconds
choices.why: Right. The name no longer resolved, so the call failed at once.

choices.text: A 200 with every unit count set to zero
choices.why: The shop does not invent counts; it says stock is unavailable.

choices.text: Nothing: the shop itself stopped as well
choices.why: The shop stayed up and answered.

choices.text: A 503, after the full two-second timeout
choices.why: The error was immediate; the timeout matters when the service hangs instead.

prompt: Why is a stock service that hangs worse for the shop than one that is stopped?
hint: How long does each make the shop wait?

choices.text: A hung service corrupts the shop's database
choices.why: The shop's data is untouched in both cases.

choices.text: A stopped service is restarted by Docker automatically within a few seconds
choices.why: The compose file sets no restart policy; that is not the difference.

choices.text: A hung service answers with wrong counts
choices.why: It does not answer at all.

choices.text: Every request waits the whole timeout instead of failing at once
choices.why: Right. Without a timeout it would wait for ever; lessons 11 and 12.

prompt: Coffee had 12 units. An order for 1 was declined by the card processor. How many units did the stock service report afterwards?
hint: The take was committed in another database before the card was tried.

prompt: The business says a declined card must never cost a unit of stock, even for a moment. Which answer does the lesson call legitimate, and cheapest?
hint: The third row of the table.

choices.text: A compensation call that puts the unit back afterwards
choices.why: That leaves a moment in which the unit is gone.

choices.text: Putting stock and payment back in one service
choices.why: Right. The boundary was in the wrong place for that requirement.

choices.text: A longer timeout on `stock_call`
choices.why: A timeout changes how long the shop waits, not whether two databases agree.

choices.text: Retrying the payment until it is accepted
choices.why: A declined card stays declined, and the unit stays gone meanwhile.

prompt: The stock team wants to rename the `units` column. Why is that hard if the shop reads the stock table directly?
hint: What became part of the contract?

choices.text: SQLite cannot rename columns
choices.why: It can; the problem is who depends on the name.

choices.text: The column is used as a primary key
choices.why: `units` is a count, not a key.

choices.text: Every query that reads it, in another service, must change in the same release
choices.why: Right. Every shared column is part of an unwritten contract.

choices.text: The shop caches the column name
choices.why: Nothing caches names; the queries are written with it.

prompt: Match each way of getting another service's data to what it depends on.
hint: The table in the middle of the section.

pairs.right: the other service up and fast on every request
a copy job and a schema kept in step

prompt: In the lab, what stops the shop from opening `stock.db`?
hint: Where does the file live?

choices.text: A password on the database file
choices.why: SQLite files have no password here.

choices.text: A firewall rule that blocks traffic between the two containers
choices.why: Nothing blocks traffic; the file simply is not there.

choices.text: A convention the shop's code follows
choices.why: It is stronger than a convention in the lab.

choices.text: It is in a volume mounted only into the stock container
choices.why: Right. The rule is physical.

prompt: Which of these does a second service add to the work, according to the lesson's table?
hint: Per service, forever.

choices.text: A second copy of the source code of the first
choices.why: Each service has its own code, not a copy of the other's.

choices.text: Its own metrics, alerts and on-call owner
choices.why: Right, among a pipeline, a deployment and an API contract.

choices.text: A larger database for the first service
choices.why: The first service's database does not grow because a second exists.

choices.text: A second programming language for the team to learn
choices.why: It allows one; it does not require one.

prompt: The lesson's table lists eight things per service. Quitanda split by every noun has 5 services. How many entries does that make?
hint: Multiply the table by the number of services.

prompt: Why does the lesson say microservices suit large organisations better than small ones?
hint: Who brings the per-service cost down, and what does that cost?

choices.text: Large organisations get discounts from cloud providers
choices.why: Prices are not the argument.

choices.text: Small organisations cannot run containers
choices.why: They can, as this lab shows.

choices.text: Large organisations have no need for transactions
choices.why: Every organisation needs them; services make them harder.

choices.text: A platform team lowers the per-service cost, and that team is itself a cost
choices.why: Right. Only a large organisation spreads that cost over enough services.

prompt: What is a distributed monolith?
hint: The costs of one, the coupling of the other.

choices.text: A monolith copied to several data centres, one copy in each
choices.why: Copies of one program are still one program, not a split.

choices.text: Services that still cannot deploy, change or fail alone
choices.why: Right: network costs with monolith coupling.

choices.text: A monolith whose modules have strong boundaries
choices.why: That is a modular monolith, the good shape of lesson 1.

choices.text: Any system with more than ten services running in production
choices.why: The count does not decide it; independence does.

prompt: Four services in a synchronous chain each answer 99.9% of the time. At most, what percentage of the time does the chain answer? Give two decimal places.
hint: Multiply 0.999 by itself four times.

prompt: A team finds that orders and stock have been released together in every one of the last twenty releases. What does the lesson suggest?
hint: The cheapest fix available.

choices.text: Split them further into smaller services
choices.why: Smaller pieces of the same coupling make it worse.

choices.text: Merge them back into one service
choices.why: Right. They always change together, so they are one.

choices.text: Put a message queue between them so they no longer call each other directly
choices.why: A queue changes how they talk; they would still have to be released together.

choices.text: Keep a spreadsheet of compatible versions
choices.why: That is a mark of the problem, not a fix for it.

prompt: Quitanda's delivery team wants to split delivery out. Delivery reads the order's address, the products' weights and whether they travel cold. Which arrangement keeps delivery independent?
hint: Who owns the weight and the cold chain?

choices.text: Delivery reads the shop's `orders` and `products` tables directly
choices.why: That makes the shop's columns part of delivery's contract.

choices.text: Delivery and the shop share a new database built for both
choices.why: A shared database is the coupling the split is meant to remove.

choices.text: Delivery calls the shop for every field, on every screen
choices.why: Possible, and it makes delivery depend on the shop being up and fast everywhere.

choices.text: Delivery owns weight and cold chain; the shop sends it the address with each order
choices.why: Right. Each owns its meaning, and only ids and the order's data cross.

prompt: Put the steps of the lab's paid order in the order they happened.
hint: Read `orders_place` from the top.
trap: The stock is committed before the card is tried, which is why a declined card loses a unit.
items: The shop reads the price from its own products table
The shop asks the stock service to take the units
The stock service commits the take in stock.db
The shop writes the order and charges the card
The shop commits its own transaction and answers 201

prompt: What did the split of the stock buy Quitanda, given the force named at the start of the lesson?
hint: The stock team of two and its schedule.

choices.text: Faster catalogue pages
choices.why: The catalogue got slower: it now makes an HTTP call.

choices.text: Atomic orders across stock and payment
choices.why: That is exactly what it lost.

choices.text: The stock team releasing on its own schedule
choices.why: Right. That was the force, and it is the only thing the split was for.

choices.text: Less memory used by the whole system, now spread over two processes
choices.why: Two processes use more than one.
